Section number: 1
Section title: Introduction and purpose
Section text:
1.1 This policy statement sets out the final rules and guidance on operational resilience and the management of third-party technology risk for firms authorised by the Financial Services Oversight Authority. It follows Consultation Paper CP25/11, which closed in March 2026, and reflects the feedback we received from firms, trade bodies and consumer groups.

1.2 Disruption to financial services can cause serious harm to consumers and to market integrity. Recent incidents have shown that firms increasingly depend on a small number of technology providers, and that an outage at one provider can affect many firms at the same time. Firms have also told us that they find it hard to assess the resilience of services they do not run themselves.

1.3 Our objective is that firms can continue to deliver their most important services through severe but plausible disruption, and that when disruption does happen, it is contained, reported promptly and learned from. We expect firms to treat operational resilience as a matter for the board, not only for technology teams.

1.4 This policy statement takes effect on 1 January 2027. The deadlines for individual requirements are set out in the relevant sections, and transitional arrangements for some firms are set out in section 9.

1.5 We will review the effectiveness of these rules two years after they take effect, and we will publish our findings.

Section number: 2
Section title: Scope and application
Section text:
2.1 This policy statement applies to all banks, building societies, payment institutions and electronic money institutions authorised by the FSOA.

2.2 It applies to the firm's activities in all jurisdictions where the failure of an activity could cause harm to consumers in our jurisdiction or to the stability of our financial system.

2.3 Some requirements are applied proportionately. For the purposes of this policy statement, a small firm is a firm that has fewer than 250,000 customers and total assets of less than £5 billion on 31 December 2026. A firm that exceeds either threshold is not a small firm.

2.4 A firm that becomes a small firm, or stops being a small firm, after 31 December 2026 must notify the FSOA within 30 days of the change. Its status for the purposes of the transitional arrangements in section 9 is fixed on 31 December 2026 and does not change.

2.5 Groups may meet these requirements at group level, provided that each authorised firm in the group can show how the group arrangements apply to its own important business services.

Section number: 3
Section title: Definitions
Section text:
3.1 An important business service is a service that a firm provides to an external end user, where disruption to the service could cause intolerable harm to consumers or risk to market integrity. Internal services, such as human resources or internal reporting, are not important business services on their own.

3.2 An impact tolerance is the maximum tolerable level of disruption to an important business service, expressed as a maximum length of time and, where relevant, a maximum number of affected customers or transactions.

3.3 A material third-party provider is a provider of technology services whose failure would cause the firm to breach an impact tolerance for one or more important business services.

3.4 A major incident is an operational incident that has caused, or is likely to cause, a breach of an impact tolerance, or that affects more than 10% of the firm's customers.

3.5 Business days are days other than weekends and public holidays in our jurisdiction.

Section number: 4
Section title: Important business services and impact tolerances
Section text:
4.1 Firms must identify their important business services by 31 March 2027. In doing so, firms should consider the number and type of customers using each service, the availability of alternatives, and the time sensitivity of payments or other transactions.

4.2 Firms must set an impact tolerance for each important business service by 31 March 2027. Impact tolerances must be set at the point at which harm becomes intolerable, not at the point at which the firm expects to be able to recover.

4.3 The board must approve the list of important business services and their impact tolerances, and must review both at least once every 12 months, or sooner if there is a material change to the firm's business.

4.4 We expect most retail banks to identify between 6 and 15 important business services. Firms that identify fewer than 4 should be prepared to explain why.

4.5 Firms must keep a record of how they identified each important business service and set each impact tolerance, and must provide it to the FSOA on request within 10 business days.

Section number: 5
Section title: Mapping and scenario testing
Section text:
5.1 Firms must map the people, processes, technology, facilities and information that support each important business service, including those provided by third parties, by 31 March 2027.

5.2 Mapping must be detailed enough to identify single points of failure and concentrations of risk, including where several important business services depend on the same third-party provider.

5.3 Firms must test their ability to remain within impact tolerance under severe but plausible scenarios. The first round of scenario testing must be completed by 30 September 2027, and testing must be repeated at least once a year after that.

5.4 Scenarios must include, at a minimum, the failure of a material third-party provider, a cyber attack that makes key systems unavailable, and the loss of a key site.

5.5 Where testing shows that a firm cannot remain within an impact tolerance, the firm must record the vulnerability, set out the actions it will take to address it, and report the vulnerability to the board at its next meeting.

Section number: 6
Section title: Third-party technology providers
Section text:
6.1 Firms must maintain a register of all material third-party providers by 31 March 2027. The register must record, for each provider, the services it supports, the data it holds, its location, and the date the contract expires.

6.2 Firms must notify the FSOA at least 60 days before entering into a new arrangement with a material third-party provider, or materially changing an existing one.

6.3 Contracts with material third-party providers must give the firm and the FSOA rights of access and audit, require the provider to report incidents to the firm without undue delay, and set out how the service will be transferred or wound down if the arrangement ends.

6.4 Firms must have a documented exit plan for each material third-party provider and must test each exit plan at least once every two years.

6.5 Where a firm uses the same material third-party provider for more than one important business service, it must assess the concentration risk and explain to the board how it would manage the failure of that provider.

6.6 Firms remain fully responsible for meeting their regulatory obligations when they outsource. Outsourcing a service does not transfer the firm's responsibility for it.

Section number: 7
Section title: Incident reporting
Section text:
7.1 Firms must submit an initial notification to the FSOA within 4 hours of classifying an incident as a major incident, and in any case no later than 24 hours after the incident is first detected.

7.2 Firms must submit an intermediate report within 72 hours of the initial notification, setting out the cause of the incident as far as it is known, the services and customers affected, and the actions taken so far.

7.3 Firms must submit a final report within 30 business days of the incident being resolved. The final report must include a root-cause analysis and the lessons learned.

7.4 Where a major incident is caused by a third-party provider, the firm remains responsible for reporting it. Firms should not delay a notification while they wait for information from the provider.

7.5 We will publish an incident reporting template before the rules take effect. Until then, firms may use their existing incident reporting formats.

Section number: 8
Section title: Governance and accountability
Section text:
8.1 Firms must name a senior manager who is responsible for operational resilience by 31 January 2027, and must notify the FSOA of that person's name within 14 days of appointing them.

8.2 Firms must complete an annual self-assessment of their operational resilience, which must be approved by the board. The first self-assessment must be completed and approved by 31 March 2028.

8.3 The self-assessment must cover the firm's important business services, impact tolerances, mapping, scenario testing results, vulnerabilities and remediation actions, and its management of material third-party providers.

8.4 Boards should receive regular management information on operational resilience, at least quarterly, and should challenge it.

8.5 Firms must keep each self-assessment for at least 5 years and provide it to the FSOA on request.

Section number: 9
Section title: Transitional arrangements
Section text:
9.1 Small firms, as defined in paragraph 2.3, may meet the requirements in paragraphs 4.1, 4.2, 5.1 and 6.1 by 31 March 2028 instead of 31 March 2027.

9.2 Small firms may complete their first round of scenario testing under paragraph 5.3 by 30 September 2028 instead of 30 September 2027.

9.3 For all firms, contracts with material third-party providers that were in place before 1 January 2027 must be updated to meet paragraph 6.3 at their next renewal, or by 31 December 2028, whichever is earlier.

9.4 The transitional arrangements do not apply to the incident reporting requirements in section 7 or to the requirement to name a senior manager in paragraph 8.1. These apply to all firms from 1 January 2027.

Section number: 10
Section title: Next steps and contacts
Section text:
10.1 We will host a series of webinars for firms in the first quarter of 2027 and will publish frequently asked questions on our website.

10.2 Firms with questions about this policy statement should contact their usual supervisory contact. General questions can be sent to our operational resilience team.

10.3 We will consult separately in 2027 on whether to extend these requirements to insurers and investment firms.

content.description: Text of the reply; may be empty.

anyOf.description:
Lists all files in a directory.

This is useful for exploring the filesystem and finding the right file to read or edit.
You should almost ALWAYS use this tool before using the read_file or edit_file tools.

path.description: Absolute path to the directory to list. Must be absolute, not relative.

anyOf.description:
Reads a file from the filesystem. Assume any path the user provides is valid; reading a missing file returns an error.

Usage:
- By default, it reads up to 100 lines starting from the beginning of the file. Use `offset`/`limit` to page through large files instead of reading them whole.
- A status header, `@@ field | field | ... @@`, sits above the file content, and every line after it is verbatim file content. When content is truncated, there may be an explanation before the header. Never include the header when editing.
- Speculatively batch multiple `read_file` calls in one response when several files may be useful.
- An empty file returns a system-reminder warning in place of contents.
- Large tool results may be offloaded to a file; the tool message gives the path. Read that path here, paging with `offset`/`limit`.
- Images (`.png`, `.jpg`, etc.), audio, video, and PDFs return multimodal content blocks (https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langchain/messages#multimodal).
- For images and PDFs, pagination via `offset`/`limit` is text-only - supply `file_path` only
- Always read a file before editing it.

file_path.description: Absolute path to the file to read. Must be absolute, not relative.

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to read. Use for pagination of large files.

offset.description: Line number to start reading from (0-indexed). Use for pagination of large files.

anyOf.description:
Writes content to a file. Creates the file if it does not exist; replaces it entirely if it does.

Usage:
- Use this tool when you intend to create a new file or replace the whole file. You do not need to read the file first.
- Prefer to edit existing files (with the edit_file tool) over creating new ones when possible.

content.description: The text content to write to the file. This parameter is required.

file_path.description: Absolute path where the file should be written. Must be absolute, not relative.

anyOf.description:
Performs exact string replacements in files.

Usage:
- You must read the file before editing; this tool errors otherwise.
- Preserve the exact source indentation from the read output, and never include the read status header in old_string or new_string.
- Prefer editing an existing file over creating a new one.
- Only use emojis if the user explicitly requests it.

file_path.description: Absolute path to the file to edit. Must be absolute, not relative.

new_string.description: The text to replace old_string with. Must be different from old_string.

old_string.description: The exact text to find and replace. Must be unique in the file unless replace_all is True.

replace_all.description: If True, replace all occurrences of old_string. If False (default), old_string must be unique.

anyOf.description:
Deletes a file or directory from the filesystem.

Usage:
- Permanently removes the file or directory at the given absolute path.
- Deleting a directory removes it and everything inside it, recursively. Prefer
  deleting a directory in one call over deleting each file individually.
- This cannot be undone, so only delete paths you are sure are no longer needed.

file_path.description: Absolute path to the file to delete. Must be absolute, not relative.

anyOf.description:
Find files matching a glob pattern, returning absolute paths.

Supports `*` (any characters within a path segment), `**` (any directories), `?` (single character), `[abc]` (one character from a set), and `{a,b}` (alternatives), e.g. `*.py`, `src/**/*.py`, `*.{yml,yaml}`.

A pattern without `/` matches the file name at any depth under the search root (`*.py` matches `src/app/main.py`). A pattern containing `/` matches the search-root-relative path (`src/**/*.py`). A leading `/` anchors to the search root (`/*.py` matches only top-level Python files).

Leading-dot names are only matched when the pattern segment itself starts with `.` (use `.env`, or `.github/**/*.yml`). Because `**` will not descend into dot-directories, the bare form `*.yml` is *broader* than `**/*.yml` and is usually what you want.

path.description: Base directory to search from. Defaults to the backend's default root.

pattern.description: Glob pattern to match files (e.g., '*.py', '**/*.py', '/subdir/**/*.md'). A pattern without '/' matches the file name at any depth; a pattern containing '/' matches the search-root-relative path; a leading '/' anchors to the search root ('/*.py' matches only top-level files). Leading-dot names are excluded unless the pattern segment starts with '.', so prefer the bare form '*.py' over '**/*.py' -- '**' will not descend into dot-directories like '.github'.

anyOf.description:
Search for a LITERAL text pattern across files (NOT regex).

The pattern is matched verbatim: regex metacharacters are ordinary characters, not operators. To match any of several strings, run a separate grep for each; `grep(pattern="foo|bar")` searches for the literal text "foo|bar", and `.*` or `\.` match those characters literally.

Returns matching files or content per `output_mode`. Offloaded large tool results live under the artifacts root (`/large_tool_results/` by default); grep that directory to search them when you do not know the exact path.

glob.description: Glob pattern (NOT regex) limiting which files are searched (e.g. '*.py', '*.ts'). A pattern without '/' matches the file name at any depth; a pattern containing '/' matches the search-root-relative path (e.g. 'src/**/*.py'). This is an in-tool file filter, not a call to the separate glob tool. Brace expansion (e.g. '*.{ts,tsx}') is not supported on all backends; run a separate search per extension for reliable results.

max_count.description: Optional cap on the total number of matches returned across all files. Leave unset to use the configured default. When the cap is hit, results are truncated and a note says so; narrow the pattern or path to see the rest.

output_mode.description: Shape of the returned text. 'files_with_matches' (default): newline-separated matching file paths. 'content': matching lines grouped by file under a '<path>:' header, each line indented and formatted '<line_number>: <line text>' (only the matched line, no surrounding context). 'count': one '<path>: <match_count>' line per file.

path.description: Directory to search in. Defaults to current working directory.

pattern.description: Text pattern to search for (literal string, not regex).

anyOf.description:
Launch an ephemeral subagent to handle a complex, multi-step task.

Available agent types and the tools they have access to:
- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for files and content, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. This agent has access to all tools as the main agent.
- section-summariser: Summarises ONE section of a regulatory document and extracts its obligations. Pass the section's number, title and full text in the task description. Returns a SectionSummary.

Specify subagent_type to select the agent. Usage notes:
- Launch multiple agents concurrently when their tasks are independent, using a single message with multiple tool calls.
- Each invocation is stateless by default: the agent sees only the prompt you give it and returns a single final report. Put full detail in the prompt and state exactly what it should return — unless an agent type below says it inherits your conversation instead.
- The agent's report is not shown to the user; relay a summary yourself.
- Tell the agent whether to create content, analyze, or only research, since it can't necessarily see the user's intent unless it inherits your conversation, as noted per agent type below.
- If an agent's description says to use it proactively, do so without waiting to be asked.
- When only general-purpose is available, use it for any complex, context-heavy task; it has the same capabilities as the main agent.

description.description: A detailed description of the task for the subagent to perform autonomously. Include all necessary context and specify the expected output format.

subagent_type.description: The type of subagent to use. Must be one of the available agent types listed in the tool description.

anyOf.description:
A document in the library, for example "PS26-4", as a JSON object with its ID, title and sections.

    Each section has its number, title and full text.
The profile of a firm, for example "FIRM-001", as a JSON object, used to say what a document means for it.

request.system:
# Document summary agent

You are a compliance analyst summarising a regulatory document, one section at a time.
The document is split at its level-2 (`##`) headings. Each section is passed to a sub-agent, which summarises that section on
its own, so a sub-agent only ever sees one section.

## Orchestrator

Given a document ID:

1. Look up the document and read its title.
2. Split the document into sections. Each section keeps its number, title and full text.
3. Pass each section to its own `section-summariser` sub-agent. Run the sub-agents in parallel.
4. Collect one `SectionSummary` back from each sub-agent, and put them in section order.
5. Combine the section summaries into a brief for the firm. Do not add obligations that no sub-agent found, and do not
   drop any that they did.

response.content:
# PS26/4 brief for Harbour Mutual Bank (FIRM-001)

**Policy Statement PS26/4: Operational resilience and third-party technology risk.** It takes effect on 1 January 2027.

## The main points for Harbour Mutual

1. **You are not a small firm, so you get none of the small-firm extensions.** You have 1.2m customers and £9bn of assets. The limits are fewer than 250,000 customers and under £5bn of assets. Your status is fixed at 31 December 2026, so the extensions in paragraphs 9.1 and 9.2 don't apply to you. Your main deadlines are **31 March 2027** and **30 September 2027**.
2. **You have no named senior manager for operational resilience yet.** Your profile shows none. You must name one by **31 January 2027**, about 9 weeks from today, and tell the FSOA within 14 days of the appointment (8.1). This deadline has no transitional relief (9.4).
3. **NimbusCloud is a concentration risk.** Mobile banking and card payments both run on it. Paragraph 6.5 says you must assess that concentration risk and explain to the board how you would manage NimbusCloud failing. Your service mapping must also show this shared dependency (5.2), and your scenario testing must include a material provider failing (5.4).
4. **Your NimbusCloud contract renews soon.** It ends on **30 June 2027**. Contracts signed before 2027 must meet paragraph 6.3 at their next renewal or by 31 December 2028, whichever comes first (9.3). For NimbusCloud, that means the June 2027 renewal must include:
   - access and audit rights for you and the FSOA
   - a duty on NimbusCloud to report incidents to you without undue delay
   - terms for transferring or winding down the service.
   
   *This is my judgement, not the sub-agents' findings:* if the renewal counts as a new or materially changed arrangement, you must give the FSOA 60 days' notice (6.2). That means notifying by about **1 May 2027**. It's worth planning for this.
5. **PayCore's contract ends on 31 December 2029.** That is after the 31 December 2028 backstop, so PayCore's contract must meet paragraph 6.3 by **31 December 2028**.
6. **Incident reporting applies from 1 January 2027 with no transition** (9.4). The 10% customer threshold for a major incident means an incident affecting more than about 120,000 of your customers (3.4).

## Key dates

| Date | What's due |
|---|---|
| 1 Jan 2027 | Rules take effect. Incident reporting applies. |
| 31 Jan 2027 | Name the senior manager, then tell the FSOA within 14 days. |
| 31 Mar 2027 | Important business services identified; impact tolerances set; mapping done; third-party register in place. |
| about 1 May 2027 | Latest FSOA notice if the NimbusCloud renewal counts as a new or materially changed arrangement (my reading). |
| 30 Jun 2027 | NimbusCloud renewal must meet paragraph 6.3. |
| 30 Sep 2027 | First round of scenario testing done; then at least yearly. |
| 31 Mar 2028 | First board-approved self-assessment. |
| 31 Dec 2028 | Backstop for updating PayCore and any other pre-2027 contracts. |

## All obligations found, by section

**Sections 1 and 3 (introduction and definitions):** no obligations.

**Section 2 (scope)**
- 2.4: If you become, or stop being, a small firm after 31 December 2026, tell the FSOA within 30 days. Your transitional status stays fixed as of 31 December 2026.

**Section 4 (important business services and impact tolerances)**
- 4.1: Identify your important business services by 31 March 2027.
- 4.2: Set an impact tolerance for each service by 31 March 2027. Set it at the point where harm becomes intolerable, not where you expect to recover.
- 4.3: The board must approve the list of services and their tolerances. It must review both at least every 12 months, or sooner after a material change.
- 4.5: Keep a record of how you identified each service and set each tolerance. Give it to the FSOA within 10 business days of a request.
- Guidance only: 4.1 lists factors you should consider. Paragraph 4.4 expects retail banks to identify 6 to 15 services, and you should be ready to explain if you identify fewer than 4.

**Section 5 (mapping and scenario testing)**
- 5.1: Map the people, processes, technology, facilities and information behind each service, including what third parties provide, by 31 March 2027.
- 5.2: The mapping must be detailed enough to show single points of failure and concentrations of risk, including several services relying on one provider.
- 5.3: Test whether you can stay within your impact tolerances in severe but plausible scenarios. The first round is due by 30 September 2027, then at least once a year.
- 5.4: Scenarios must include at least:
  - a material third-party provider failing
  - a cyber attack that takes key systems down
  - losing a key site.
- 5.5: If a test shows you can't stay within a tolerance, record the weakness, set out how you will fix it, and report it to the board at its next meeting.

**Section 6 (third-party providers)**
- 6.1: Keep a register of material third-party providers by 31 March 2027. For each, record the services it supports, the data it holds, its location and its contract end date.
- 6.2: Tell the FSOA at least 60 days before a new arrangement with a material provider, or a material change to an existing one.
- 6.3: Contracts with material providers must include:
  - access and audit rights for you and the FSOA
  - a duty on the provider to report incidents to you without undue delay
  - terms for transferring or winding down the service.
- 6.4: Keep a documented exit plan for each material provider and test it at least every two years.
- 6.5: Where one material provider supports more than one service, assess the concentration risk and explain to the board how you would handle that provider failing.
- 6.6: You stay fully responsible for your regulatory obligations when you outsource.

**Section 7 (incident reporting)**
- 7.1: Send the FSOA an initial notification within 4 hours of classing an incident as major, and no later than 24 hours after you first detect it.
- 7.2: Send an intermediate report within 72 hours of the initial notification. It covers the cause as far as known, the services and customers affected, and the actions taken so far.
- 7.3: Send a final report within 30 business days of the incident being resolved, including a root-cause analysis and lessons learned.
- 7.4: You stay responsible for reporting a major incident even if a third party caused it. Guidance: don't delay a notification while waiting for the provider's information.
- 7.5: Until the FSOA publishes its template, you may use your existing formats.

**Section 8 (governance)**
- 8.1: Name a senior manager for operational resilience by 31 January 2027. Tell the FSOA their name within 14 days of the appointment.
- 8.2: Complete a self-assessment every year and have the board approve it. The first is due by 31 March 2028.
- 8.3: The self-assessment must cover:
  - your important business services and impact tolerances
  - mapping and scenario testing results
  - weaknesses and the actions to fix them
  - how you manage material third-party providers.
- 8.5: Keep each self-assessment for at least 5 years and give it to the FSOA on request.
- Guidance only (8.4): the board should get management information on operational resilience at least quarterly and should challenge it.

**Section 9 (transitional arrangements)**
- 9.1 and 9.2: Small firms get until 31 March 2028 for paragraphs 4.1, 4.2, 5.1 and 6.1, and until 30 September 2028 for their first scenario test. **This doesn't apply to Harbour Mutual.** The section 9 sub-agent called these "mandatory", but the text says firms "may", so they are relaxations rather than duties.
- 9.3: All firms must update pre-2027 material provider contracts to meet 6.3 at their next renewal or by 31 December 2028, whichever is earlier.
- 9.4: Incident reporting (section 7) and naming the senior manager (8.1) apply to all firms from 1 January 2027.

**Section 10 (next steps):** no obligations. The FSOA will run webinars in Q1 2027, publish FAQs, and consult in 2027 on extending the rules to insurers and investment firms.
